A warming bowl of coastal comfort
Published on November 10, 2025 | By Marion MacLeod

Background

Cullen Skink's rich history dates back to the 18th century, when it was a staple of the fishing village of Cullen in the east coast of Scotland. The dish was born out of necessity, created by housewives who would cook leftover smoked haddock and potatoes together to make a nourishing meal for their families.

Throughout the centuries, Cullen Skink has remained a beloved comfort food throughout Scotland, particularly during times of hardship. In the 19th century, it was a common sight to see women serving Cullen Skink in the local pubs, providing sustenance for weary fishermen returning from a long day at sea. The dish's reputation as a warming and satisfying meal has endured, making it a staple of Scottish cuisine.

Traditionally, Cullen Skink is served on special occasions such as Burns Night, Hogmanay, or when visiting family in the north-east of Scotland. Its hearty flavour and comforting warmth make it an ideal dish to share with loved ones, evoking memories of cold winter nights by the fire and tales of the sea.

Ingredients

  • Smoked haddock — 450g / 16oz
  • Milk — 300ml / 10fl oz
  • Potatoes — 200g / 7oz
  • Onions — 100g / 4oz
  • Dill — 30g / 1oz
  • Garlic — 15g / 1oz

Method

  1. Place the smoked haddock in a large saucepan and cover with cold water. Bring to a gentle boil over medium heat - this helps to remove excess saltiness and prepare the fish for flaking. You'll know it's ready when the fish easily flakes apart with a fork, usually after about 5-7 minutes. Don't let it boil vigorously as this can make the fish tough. Once cooked, carefully remove the fish and set aside, reserving the cooking liquid as it adds depth to the final dish.
    5-7 minutes medium
  2. In a separate saucepan, combine the peeled and diced potatoes, chopped onion, and minced garlic. Add enough cold water to cover the ingredients. Bring the mixture to a boil over high heat, then reduce to low heat and simmer for 15-20 minutes or until the potatoes are tender.
    15-20 minutes low
  3. Add the milk to the potato mixture and stir well. Continue to simmer over low heat for an additional 5 minutes, allowing the creamy sauce to thicken.
    5 minutes low
  4. Carefully add the cooked smoked haddock back into the saucepan with the potato mixture. Stir gently to combine, being careful not to break up the fish flakes. Bring the mixture to a gentle simmer over low heat.
    low
  5. Stir in the chopped fresh dill and cook for an additional 1-2 minutes, allowing the flavors to meld together. Taste and adjust seasoning as needed.
    1-2 minutes low
  6. Serve the Cullen Skink hot, garnished with additional chopped fresh dill if desired. Traditionally served in bowls or cauldrons, enjoy warm and comforting!

Variations

Smoked Haddock Upgrade

Using premium smoked haddock for enhanced flavor

  • Using 500g of premium smoked haddock instead of the recommended 450g

Whole Potato Variation

Using whole potatoes for a heartier soup

  • Adding 2-3 medium-sized whole potatoes to the pot during step 1, instead of diced potatoes

Serving Suggestions

Traditional

Serve hot, garnished with chopped fresh dill. Traditionally, Cullen Skink is served in small bowls or ramekins and accompanied by crusty bread for dipping into the creamy broth.

  • crusty bread
  • dried biscuits

Drinks

A glass of white wine, such as Chardonnay or Sauvignon Blanc, pairs nicely with Cullen Skink's rich flavours. For a more Scottish experience, try pairing it with a glass of Irn-Bru or a whisky on the rocks.

  • Irn-Bru
  • whisky
